newsitem.title: THAILAND: Outlook bleak as Thai stocks continue to tumble.
newsitem.headline: Outlook bleak as Thai stocks continue to tumble.

text.p: Thai stocks, driven to their lowest levels in more than 5-1/2 years this week by a slew of negative factors, will remain under pressure in the short term, analysts and traders said on Wednesday.
While record highs in U.S. and British stocks have buoyed most Asian markets in recent days, the composite Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index has been pummeled.
The index took a further battering on Wednesday, shedding 2.60 percent to close at 626.57, a new 5-1/2 year low.
The market has lost more than 52 percent of its value from its close on May 7, 1996, when it stood at 1,319.20.

Economic concerns underpin the present slide, but a series of related factors, most significantly worries surrounding loan portfolio quality and lower corporate earnings prospects, are also weighing heavily on sentiment.
"This doesn't look like it is going to be a good year for the Thai economy," said Somchai Trairattanapirom, vice president at Sitca Investment and Securities.

"From an optimistic view perhaps the SET index can stand above 600 but since we have to follow the Bank of Thailand's (economic) indicators, they don't give us such a good picture and it is possible the market will go below 600," he said.

Weakening economic growth, forecast by private-sector analysts to slow to five percent this year -- its lowest level since 1986 -- is putting increasing pressure on corporate earnings prospects, analysts said.

Bank of Thailand executives have said the economy has yet to reach the bottom of the economic cycle and hopes of an export- led recovery in the second half of the year are looking less likely as first quarter export figures for February showed a 5.5 percent year-on-year decline, analysts said.
Thai corporations are already being squeezed by high financing costs. Minimum lending rates are among the highest in the region at 12.75 percent.
But lower growth looks likely to hit even the profits of sectors not sensitive to interest rates, such as energy, analysts said.

Interest rates, which fell 25 basis points last week, cannot be lowered sufficiently to strongly stimulate the ailing economy because the Thai baht is about 80 percent pegged to the U.S. dollar and the Bank of Thailand has pledged to defend its currency.
"The macro situation is having an impact at the micro level and causing a lot of problems," said a senior economist at a local brokerage.
The problems could worsen as declining earnings reduce government tax revenues, which could force the government to further cut spending if it is to balance the fiscal budget, analysts said.
"We expect that the government may have to announce further (spending) cuts given the declining revenues from tax collection," the economist said.

Loan portfolio quality in the bank, finance and securities sectors is once again a growing concern among investors due to the central bank's ruling that firms must release non-performing loan figures at the end of the second quarter, analysts said.
A property slump and deteriorating lending environment have many investors fearful about companies with high exposure to property sector and car-purchase loans.
Some firms are said to have a combined exposure to these sectors of over 40 percent, analysts said. ($1 = 26 baht)
